description: We’re a multidisciplinary team exploring astronaut health, space nutrition, food science, and AI-driven innovation. Our goal is to develop practical tools connecting astronaut health data with nutrition and mission conditions. We bring expertise in nutrition, food science, and research and welcome teammates in AI/ML, software, data science, UX/UI, and visualization.
summary:
SageCare is a crew-facing health-monitoring web prototype developed for the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". It brings daily nutrition and hydration, sleep and wellbeing check-ins, cardiovascular measurements, exercise records, EVA atmosphere and preparation context, and radiation-exposure information into one astronaut workflow.

Its central feature is For You: a daily priorities view that connects recorded information to clear, understandable points for attention, for example, nutrient intake against a target range, fluid intake against a daily minimum, sleep against a scheduled opportunity, and resting heart rate against the crew member’s own baseline. Rather than relying on a single opaque health score, SageCare keeps the underlying measurements and their context visible.

As missions travel farther from Earth, crews need organised ways to review their health and daily countermeasures when immediate ground support and resupply may be constrained. SageCare demonstrates how these different records could be brought together in a crew-side workspace, using NASA human-spaceflight research and standards as references.

The current public version is a prototype with sample profiles, simulated telemetry and crew-entered records. It is not a connected flight medical system or a diagnostic device.
details:
1. The problem we are addressing

Long-duration space missions place several demands on the human body at the same time. Crew members must maintain adequate nutrition and hydration, manage sleep and workload, preserve physical fitness, review physiological measurements, and prepare for operations such as extravehicular activity (EVA). Radiation exposure and the constraints of an isolated, closed environment add further challenges.

These responsibilities become more difficult when a crew is far from Earth. Measurements, daily routines and countermeasures may be recorded in different places, making it harder for a crew member to see how the different parts of their daily health picture relate to one another.

SageCare addresses this organisational problem: how can an astronaut review relevant health measurements and daily countermeasure records in one understandable, crew-facing workspace?

2. What SageCare does

SageCare is designed around a crew member’s mission day. The public prototype brings together the following functions.

A. For You: daily priorities at a glance

The home screen brings selected information from different modules into one view. It highlights points such as nutrient intake relative to a target range, hydration progress, sleep duration and resting heart rate relative to a personal reference.

This is an important design choice: SageCare does not hide the data behind a single wellness score. It shows the measurement, its relevant context and the related NASA Human Research Roadmap risk references. The aim is to help the crew member understand what a recorded value means in context and where to review it in more detail.

A daily wellbeing check-in is also included to provide a simple way to record how the crew member is feeling.

B. Nutrition and hydration: daily countermeasures

Nutrition is one of SageCare’s main areas of focus. The nutrition module includes:

  • An estimated energy requirement calculated from crew profile information.
  • Daily protein, carbohydrate, fat, fibre and fluid targets.
  • Food search, food selection, meal categorisation and portion selection.
  • A daily food log with energy and macronutrient progress.
  • Fluid-intake tracking, including a 250 mL quick-add function.
  • A space-food reference catalogue that includes scrambled eggs, chicken-pineapple salad, and Artemis II menu examples such as almonds and cashews.

The module separates nutritional targets from recorded intake. A calculated requirement is not treated as food that has already been consumed. Food records also indicate whether their values come from USDA references, provided reference values or illustrative estimates.

The purpose is to make nutrition and hydration part of routine health monitoring rather than treating food as a separate logistical concern.

C. Personal health monitoring: measurements, context and trends

The monitoring module presents cardiovascular and recovery information, including:

  • Heart rate and resting-heart-rate context.
  • Heart-rate variability (HRV), with the displayed metric identified as SDNN.
  • Blood pressure readings and a history view.
  • Sleep records, a manual sleep diary and a seven-day sleep overview.
  • Personal reference values and measurement context where available.

The interface distinguishes scheduled sleep opportunities from actual recorded sleep. It also encourages comparison with an individual’s own reference rather than assuming that one general value is appropriate for every astronaut.

D. Exercise countermeasures

The exercise module provides a structured session-recording interface. It includes fields for exercise type, duration, exercise name, load, sets and repetitions, with additional fields for heart rate and equipment-derived force or torque when available.

Resistance-training records can be organised by exercise so that comparable sessions can be reviewed over time. This is intended to support the monitoring of exercise countermeasures during missions in which maintaining physical fitness is important.

The prototype does not claim to measure bone density, muscle mass or strength from heart rate or calorie estimates. Those outcomes require appropriate measurements and validated equipment.

E. EVA preparation and environmental monitoring

The EVA section brings preparation records and environmental parameters into the same monitoring workspace. It includes an EVA preparation checklist, pre-breathe and pressure-transition record fields, and a post-EVA symptom check-in.

The atmospheric display deliberately distinguishes between different measurements, including blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), raw suit oxygen partial pressure (ppO₂), inspired oxygen partial pressure (PIO₂), raw suit carbon dioxide partial pressure (ppCO₂), inspired carbon dioxide partial pressure (PICO₂), and suit pressure.

These values are shown with their own units and context. For example, a blood oxygen saturation value is not treated as interchangeable with a spacesuit oxygen measurement, and inspired carbon dioxide reference durations are not applied to raw suit gas values without a validated conversion.

F. Radiation and research context

The monitoring page includes a radiation-exposure interface with timestamped sample values and mission-exposure context. It also provides an entry point for searching NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) study metadata.

These sections are intended to show how relevant environmental and research context could sit alongside the crew member’s health records. The radiation values currently displayed are simulated examples, not live personal dosimeter readings or imported NASA telemetry.

3. What makes SageCare different

SageCare’s main contribution is not simply displaying multiple health measurements. It connects daily countermeasures with health-monitoring context.

For example, a crew member can review nutrition and hydration, check sleep and cardiovascular trends, record an exercise session and consult EVA-related information within the same application. The For You view makes selected priorities easier to recognise without replacing the underlying measurements with an unexplained score.

The project also places emphasis on measurement context and transparency:

  • Measurements are displayed with units and timestamps where available.
  • Personal baselines are kept distinct from general reference values.
  • Targets are not mistaken for actual intake.
  • Scheduled sleep opportunity is not presented as actual sleep.
  • Blood oxygen and suit-atmosphere measurements are kept separate.
  • Simulated and manually entered values are identified as such.

These distinctions matter in a health-monitoring interface, where presenting a number without its source, conditions or appropriate reference can lead to misleading conclusions.

4. Potential impact

SageCare could help astronauts maintain a clearer view of their daily health-related records and countermeasures during long-duration missions. By reducing fragmentation between nutrition, hydration, sleep, exercise and physiological measurements, it aims to make routine self-monitoring more understandable and consistent.

Its nutrition-centred approach is particularly relevant because food and fluid intake are modifiable parts of daily mission life. The NASA Human Research Roadmap identifies inadequate food and nutrition as a risk to crew performance and health while also highlighting the constraints of providing safe, acceptable and nutritionally adequate food for exploration missions.

The same crew-side approach could eventually support ground medical teams by making organised, timestamped records easier to review when communication is delayed. That is a future operational use case, not a capability claimed as fully implemented in this prototype.

5. Development and technical approach

The project is developed as a browser-based crew application, deployed publicly through Vercel, with its source code and documentation maintained in GitHub.

The project repository describes a web technology stack built around Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, with charting components including ECharts and Recharts. It also documents a broader target architecture involving Python/FastAPI, WebSockets, MQTT, PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB and offline data handling. These backend and connectivity elements represent the project's development direction and should not be interpreted as proof that live sensor ingestion, a complete ground-station system or fully tested delay-tolerant synchronisation is available in the current public prototype.

6. Current prototype scope and limitations

The deployed application is a prototype, not a flight-qualified or clinically validated system.

  • The displayed crew profile and physiological telemetry are sample or simulated data.
  • Health and EVA records can be entered through the prototype interfaces; no real wearable, spacesuit/PLSS, CANS or individual radiation dosimeter is connected.
  • No raw NASA RadLab or Environmental Data Application telemetry is currently imported into the application.
  • The OSDR feature provides a study-metadata search entry point; it does not mean that a NASA physiological dataset has already been integrated into the app's calculations.
  • The food catalogue contains a mixture of reference values and demonstration estimates. Complete micronutrient-intake coverage is not yet available.
  • Barcode scanning, live hardware integrations, fully tested offline synchronisation and a complete ground-side monitoring console remain future development areas.

SageCare does not diagnose medical conditions, determine whether an astronaut is fit for duty, or prescribe treatment. Any operational version would require mission-specific requirements, validated hardware and data interfaces, medical oversight, security controls and appropriate verification.

Project Details

Technical Stack

The deployed crew-facing application is built with Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript, with Tailwind CSS for styling. It supports Supabase-backed storage when configured, with a local SQLite fallback for development. Vitest is included for testing, and the web application is deployed through Vercel.

The repository also contains Python service dependencies for a broader planned architecture, including FastAPI, WebSockets, MQTT and PostgreSQL-related tools. These are separate from the currently deployed crew application and should not be interpreted as proof of live sensor connectivity or a running ground-station system.

Implemented Features

The current prototype provides:

  • A crew-facing dashboard with daily health and countermeasure context.
  • An estimated energy requirement calculator and daily nutrition targets.
  • A food catalogue, food logging, portion selection and macronutrient tracking.
  • Fluid-intake tracking.
  • Cardiovascular measurement views, including heart rate, HRV and blood pressure.
  • Sleep records and sleep-trend views.
  • An exercise-session recording interface.
  • EVA preparation and atmospheric-monitoring interfaces.
  • Radiation-monitoring displays using clearly identified sample values.
  • NASA OSDR study-metadata search.

The application supports persistent storage through Supabase when configured, while retaining a local SQLite fallback. The deployed storage configuration and end-to-end save/update behaviour should be tested before these are demonstrated as completed interactions.

Methodology

Our development process began by mapping NASA's five human-spaceflight hazards—space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile or closed environments—to relevant astronaut health risks and monitoring needs.

We then organised the interface around a crew member's daily mission workflow, connecting nutrition, hydration, sleep, exercise, cardiovascular measurements and EVA context. NASA Human Research Roadmap risks, NASA-STD-3001 and relevant NASA technical briefs informed the selection and interpretation of these monitoring categories.

A key design principle is to preserve the distinction between measured or entered records, calculated targets and simulated values. The prototype is intended to support informed review of health information, not replace medical judgement or mission-approved procedures.

Limitations

SageCare is an early-stage prototype, not a flight-qualified or clinically validated medical system.

  • Physiological and environmental readings are simulated or manually entered; no live wearable, exercise-device, spacesuit/PLSS, CANS or individual radiation-dosimeter feed is connected.
  • NASA OSDR functionality searches study metadata; private astronaut medical records and raw research datasets are not imported into the app's calculations.
  • The radiation display does not represent live NASA RadLab telemetry or individual crew dose.
  • Complete micronutrient-intake coverage is not yet available across the food catalogue.
  • Robust offline synchronisation, live sensor ingestion and a connected base-station console remain future development areas.
  • The current prototype has no user sign-in. Real personal or medical data must not be entered until authentication, access controls and deployment security have been implemented and validated.

SageCare is designed to inform and organise health-monitoring information. It does not diagnose medical conditions, determine fitness for duty or prescribe treatment.

Link: https://github.com/Space-Spider-Team/Space-Spider

7. Future development

The next development stage would focus on connecting validated wearable, exercise-device, spacesuit and radiation-monitoring sources; improving NASA dataset integration; completing the food and micronutrient database; and validating secure offline and delayed-communication workflows.

The longer-term goal is a reliable crew-side health-monitoring workspace that helps astronauts and authorised medical teams review measurements and everyday countermeasures together throughout deep-space missions.


AI & Tool Disclosure

ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used as an assisting tool for research support, scientific literature exploration, documentation, content refinement and presentation preparation. AI was not used to originate the team's core solution concept. The project direction, feature selection, scientific interpretation and final implementation decisions were led by the team. All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and adapted by the team.
